newsitem.title: UK: UK RPI data point to new year rate rise - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK RPI data point to new year rate rise - analysts.

text.p: Strong November RPI data will increase the likelihood of a further rise in official British interest rates early in the new year, economists said.
"The underlying picture still looks the same. The inflation target is beginning to look unattainable and there is a strong case for a January rate rise," said Ian Stewart, a Merrill Lynch economist.
Rates appear to be on hold at 6.0 percent this month. The Bank of England made no announcement when it forecast the daily money market shortage at 0945 GMT.

Inflation rose 0.1 percent in November, leaving the year-on- year rate at 2.7 percent, unchanged from October. Underlying inflation stuck stubbornly at 3.3 percent for the second month running, still some way above the official 2.5 percent target.
Economists were unsurprised that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George decided to leave rates on hold after their meeting on Wednesday.
It is too soon after the budget for Clarke to agree to a rate rise, and George's comments to the Treasury select committee suggested he was not going to push too hard for a move, Stewart said.
Marian Bell, treasury economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, said Clarke is playing a dangerous game if he delays a further rate rise for much longer.
"The Chancellor...runs the risk of inflicting larger and more freqent hikes in rates the longer he leaves this one," she said.
Bell believes the government will miss its inflation target.
"Today's data give the lie to the government's assertion that October's rise was a blip. Nor do we forecast significantly lower inflation from next month on."
When underlying inflation hit 3.3 percent in October, from 2.9 percent in September, the government said the low level of inflation in October 1995 exaggerated the rise.
This time, the government said the impact of lower factory gate prices was yet to be fully felt on the high street.
While costs are certainly very weak, the danger is that retailers will not pass them on to consumers, but instead push through higher prices because demand is so strong.
The breakdown on November's figures show price sensitivity in some sectors may be waning. Clothing and footwear prices rose 1.1 percent in the month after being unchanged in October.
Household goods prices gained 1.0 percent in the month and were up 2.5 percent on the year.

But food prices, which benefited from a strong pound and lower input prices, helped to offset these price rises. Seasonal food prices fell 0.6 percent in November and non-seasonal food fell by 0.3 percent.
"Maybe next month we may see some bonus from slightly softer oil prices which are coming through," Adrian Owens, economist at Julius Baer Investments, told Reuters Financial Television.
"Cost pressures are still quite positive and conducive to lower inflation."
He sees RPIX dropping to a low of 2.8 percent in the autumn before heading higher again.
Andrew Milligan of General Accident sees RPIX slowly decelerating towards 2.75 percent in the first half of next year, but cautions:
"This assumes that there is not much further widening of retail margins, that oil prices fall away but that sterling holds onto most of its recent gains."
